title: Springs and Shellmounds Above the Cove

place.label: Sutro Baths Upper Trail, Lands End

hook: Long before Sutro's glass palace, Yelamu Ohlone families camped above this cove, drinking from hillside springs that still trickle down into the ruins.
story: Before there was a Cliff House, a toll road or a single numbered avenue, this windy headland belonged to the Yelamu, a tribal group of the Ramaytush Ohlone, the people of the western side of the bay [2]. Their main villages lay near Mission Creek, Visitacion Valley and today's Crissy Field, but Lands End was a seasonal camp [2]. Here they found fresh water from hillside springs, brush and trees for shelters, and a shore rich in otters, sea lions and sea birds; they also played stick games and told stories [1]. Some of those springs still run just below the Lands End Lookout, down into the old Sutro Baths pools, and a shellmound, or midden, of shells, bones and seeds survives beside the Sutro Baths Upper Trail [2]. The National Park Service notes that Spanish settlement of San Francisco, which began in 1776, ended the Yelamu's traditional life here [1]. Under Mexican rule the coast became part of a land grant, Rancho Punta de Lobos [1]. The next time crowds came to this cove, they would arrive by toll road to gawk at the sea lions.

title: A Toll Road, a Roadhouse and a Rope
hook: On July 4, 1863, a plain clapboard bar opened on the cliff. Three years later a woman walked a tightrope from it to Seal Rocks.
story: The Cliff House was born as a real-estate play. Speculator Charles C. Butler built it alongside the new Point Lobos Toll Road, backed by State Senator John P. Buckley, an officer of the road company [1]. It opened on July 4, 1863, with the well-known host Captain Junius G. Foster in charge. Despite being called a hotel, it served only food and drink, and the real draw was the view of the sea lions on the rocks below [1]. Omnibuses left Kearny and Clay streets for the seals at 50 cents a ride, and drivers paid a toll near today's Masonic Avenue [2]. Early-morning carriage rides out for breakfast became the fashion; Mark Twain made the trip in 1864 and wrote a grumpy, funny account [1]. When the view wasn't enough, Foster booked balloon ascensions and acrobats. On June 24, 1866, Miss Rosa Celeste walked a 400-foot rope from the cliff to Seal Rocks, 100 feet above the surf and without guide wires, while five thousand people watched [1]. Presidents Grant and Hayes later came to dine [1].

title: Trotters Racing Down Point Lobos Road

place.label: Geary Blvd (old Point Lobos Road) west of 23rd Ave

hook: Before houses, today's Geary Boulevard was a toll road through sand, with a half-mile racetrack for San Francisco's fastest horses laid along it.
story: Geary Boulevard began life as the Point Lobos Road, a private toll road opened in the early 1860s that was, for years, the fashionable drive out of the city [1]. Drivers paid at a toll house near today's Masonic Avenue, received a ticket and dropped it at a second gate before the road ran downhill to the Cliff House [1]. Around 1875 ('about twenty years ago', wrote the San Francisco Call in 1895), the road's operators tried to make the trip more exciting by building a straightaway half-mile speed track on the north side of the road, starting at the line of 23rd Avenue [1]. Some of the best horses of the day, including Norfolk and Lodi, were run there. Nearby, horseman Jim Eoff opened an Agricultural Park race track, which did not succeed [1]. The Western Neighborhoods Project describes the area of that era as foggy sand and scrub with roadhouses, racetracks and dairymen [2]. As the city crept west, the toll gates came down, streetcars replaced omnibuses, and in 1895 the dissolved road company auctioned its last 160 Richmond District lots [1].

title: The Night the Dynamite Ship Blew

place.label: Cove below the Cliff House (Parallel Point)

hook: An abandoned schooner packed with forty tons of dynamite drifted onto the rocks below the Cliff House. At 12:30 a.m., it was felt in Sacramento.
story: The schooner Parallel left a San Francisco wharf on Wednesday, January 12, 1887, bound for Oregon and illegally packed with a cargo that included forty tons of dynamite powder [1]. Three days of bad weather left her no farther than Lands End. On Saturday evening, caught in a heavy swell, the crew rowed for safety without sending any warning [1]. The empty ship drifted onto a rock in the cove below the Cliff House. Adolph Sutro and other locals went down to help but found no one aboard and went home to wait for morning [2]. Just after midnight on Sunday, January 16, the cargo exploded. The blast was felt as far away as Sacramento, Vacaville and San Jose; the crew watched from Point Bonita across the Gate [1]. The Cliff House lost a wing and most of its windows [3]. Seal Rock House, Sutro Heights and nearby cottages were hit by debris [1]. Nobody died. The next day a crowd estimated as high as 80,000 came hunting relics, and by morning a hand-painted 'Bar Open' sign was up [1]. The bluff became known as Parallel Point [2].

title: The President Who Wouldn't Pose Twice
hook: Benjamin Harrison came to Adolph Sutro's clifftop garden, stared silently at the Golden Gate, endured one photo, and sat down to a very long, very wet lunch.
story: Adolph Sutro turned a clifftop cottage into Sutro Heights, a garden of more than twenty acres with flower beds, hedge mazes, a conservatory and over 200 concrete copies of classical statues imported from Belgium, tended by a staff of 17 [2]. Anyone could stroll it, and guests from Oscar Wilde to presidents breakfasted there [4]. On April 27, 1891, President Benjamin Harrison arrived. The Morning Call reported that he stood silently gazing at the Golden Gate, seeing it for the first time, until Sutro's hired photographer pointed a camera at him. Hands in overcoat pockets, hat pulled down, the president allowed exactly one shot and walked off [1]. Lunch ran nearly two hours: oysters, caviar, sweetbreads, roast duck, and wines including an 1872 Chateau Lafitte and 1825 cognac. The Postmaster-General turned his glass upside down [1]. Then Sutro rose and gave Harrison a photolithograph of a 1602 letter from the navigator Sebastián Vizcaíno at Monterey, which Sutro said he had found in the archives at Seville [1]. The National Park Service dates the public garden to 1885; Sutro bought the cottage in 1881 [2][3].

title: Sutro's Secondhand Amusement Park
hook: That windswept parking lot above the Sutro Baths ruins once held a Ferris-style wheel, a mirror maze and a room that swung around its riders.
story: Adolph Sutro could never pass up a bargain [1]. When the 1894 Midwinter Fair in Golden Gate Park sold off its attractions, he bought several and rebuilt them on a cleared strip just east of his baths [1]. The centrepiece was the 100-foot 'Firth Wheel', whose 16 carriages carried riders on 20-minute trips high above the baths. Across the midway stood the Mystic Maze, a house of mirrors, and the Haunted Swing: visitors sat on a gently rocking glider while the whole furnished room, mounted on gimbals, swung the other way, creating the illusion that the room was spinning around them. It was reported to be very unsettling [1]. By 1898 there was also a small 'Scenic Railway' coaster and chowder stands made from recycled fair kiosks [1][2]. The name Merrie Way came later. But the fun did not last. Sutro died in 1898, and by 1900 insurance maps marked every attraction closed or not in operation [1]. A 1910 photo shows the weather-beaten wheel above a deserted midway; after 1923 only cleared land remained [1].

title: Seven Pools Under 100,000 Panes of Glass
hook: Adolph Sutro built a glass palace where the tide filled seven pools, 10,000 swimmers could splash at once, and Egyptian mummies watched from the lobby.
story: Adolph Sutro began planning public baths in 1888, offering a $500 prize for the design, won by architects C. J. Colley and Emil S. Lemme [1]. After years of engineering, a long fight with the Southern Pacific over railway access and more than a million dollars, Sutro Baths officially opened on March 14, 1896 [1]. A classical portal led into a glass enclosure roofed with 100,000 panes over seven pools, one of cold seawater and the rest heated to different temperatures [1][2]. At high tide the ocean itself could fill the 1.7 million gallons needed in about an hour. The baths could hold 10,000 people and rented out 20,000 bathing suits and 40,000 towels [2]. Swimmers entered by slides, trapezes, flying rings and diving platforms [1]. Jerry Flamm remembered the favourite dare: dive into the hot pool, then race to the ice-cold one [1]. The lobby held stuffed animals, art and Egyptian mummies [2]. In 1913 and 1914 Duke Kahanamoku set world records there [1]. Sutro wanted cheap, healthy recreation for thousands, but the baths never made steady money [2].

title: John Harris Buys a Ticket to Swim

place.label: Sutro Baths entrance, Point Lobos Ave

hook: On the Fourth of July, 1897, a Black San Franciscan paid his quarter at Sutro Baths and was refused the water. So he sued Adolph Sutro.
story: On July 4, 1897, John Harris came to Sutro Baths with some white friends and bought a 25-cent ticket for admission, a bathing suit and a changing room. Staff refused him because he was Black. On July 11 he tried again and was turned away again [1]. Harris sued Adolph Sutro for $5,000 per refusal under the Dibble Bill, a new California civil rights law that took effect on April 29, 1897 and banned discrimination by bathhouses and other public businesses [1]. The baths' superintendent openly defended the policy: Black patrons could watch but not swim, because white customers would leave. He predicted the case would never come to trial [1]. The Assembly Club, a Black social organisation, offered to help pay for test cases like it [1]. On February 17, 1898, the Chronicle reported the result: the judge instructed the jury that it had to find for Harris. The jury awarded the minimum, $50 for each refusal. Because the verdict was under $300 Harris had to pay costs, so he gained little money [1]. The National Park Service now calls it an early civil rights victory [2].

title: Murder at the Acropolis Oyster Stand

place.label: Site of the Acropolis Chophouse (now Lands End Lookout), Point Lobos Ave

hook: Manuel Varvare served oysters from a recycled world's-fair kiosk above the baths. After he reported a robbery, the robber came back.
story: Around 1898 Manuel Varvare (his name is also spelled Varvaris and Vavare) opened the Acropolis Oyster Stand in a kiosk that Adolph Sutro had bought from the 1894 Midwinter Fair and set up on Cliff Avenue, today's Point Lobos Avenue [1]. It grew lean-tos for a kitchen, a dining room and a stand-up oyster bar, and Varvare slept in a small room at the back [1]. Business was poor after Sutro died and the nearby Merrie Way rides shut, and he twice tried to sell [1][2]. In February 1905 three soldiers refused to pay and attacked him with knives and a club [1]. On February 7, 1908, an armed robber took $87, wrote down Varvare's name, and warned he would kill him if he went to the police. Varvare reported it anyway [1]. The Call said the robber returned on a Friday night, struck him with a .45 revolver and fractured his skull. Varvare died at French Hospital on March 7, 1908; the police admitted they had no clue to the killer [1]. His fruit-stand neighbour, Nicholas Antipa, took over. The city demolished the stands in 1922 when it widened the road [1].

title: Survived the Quake, Lost to a Wire
hook: In 1906, rumours said Sutro's castle had slid into the sea. It hadn't. Seventeen months later, electricians did what the earthquake couldn't.
story: Adolph Sutro's turreted Cliff House opened in 1896, a wooden 'French chateau' with marble floors, electric lights, an elevator and twenty private dining rooms [2]. It survived the 1906 earthquake, but rumours that it had fallen into the ocean spread fast [1]. The building really was lost the next year. On September 7, 1907, while it was closed for remodelling, former proprietor James Wilkins was touring the work when he saw smoke rising through a floor where electricians had been working. He raised the alarm, got caught in the fire himself and had to be rescued [1]. The Examiner called the blaze 'something sent from the unknown to hold the human mind in awe and wonderment' [1]. Not everyone mourned: a letter to The Argonaut asked whether a score of readers had not said 'Thank Heaven!' [2]. Sutro's daughter Emma Sutro Merritt rebuilt in the post-quake spirit, with a modest fireproof building of steel-reinforced concrete that opened in 1909 and still stands [3].

title: The Last Steam Train to the Cliff

place.label: Former steam depot, 48th Ave and Point Lobos Ave

hook: Until 1905, San Franciscans rode a little steam train along the cliffs of Lands End to a depot at 48th Avenue. Thomas Edison's cameramen filmed it.
story: The Ferries and Cliff House steam line ran from California Street and Central Avenue (now Presidio Avenue) out California Street to 33rd Avenue, then swung north along the cliffs above the Golden Gate to a terminus above the Cliff House at 48th Avenue and Point Lobos [1]. It was built by the Powell Street cable railway to give it a route to the beach. Sources disagree on its opening, giving both 1886 and 1888 [1]. Its double-ended locomotives needed no turntables, and the route passed through two tunnels [1]. On January 11, 1902, a camera crew from Thomas Edison's company filmed the train on the coast [1]. From the depot, visitors walked downhill past souvenir stands to the Cliff House and Sutro Baths [2]. The last steam trains ran on May 17, 1905, the last steam-powered streetcar line in the city, when United Railroads rebuilt the route for electric streetcars [1][3]. The cliffs had the final word: after a landslide on February 7, 1925, the tracks along Lands End were abandoned [1].

title: The Richmond Refuses to Become Spanish Town
hook: In 1909 the city voted to rename every numbered avenue in Spanish, from Arguello to Zamorano. The Richmond revolted within a week.
story: After the 1906 earthquake, the Post Office struggled with two sets of numbered streets. In 1909 a city commission proposed replacing the Richmond and Sunset's numbered avenues with Spanish names in alphabetical order, running from Arguello to Zamorano and then on to Spanish saints beyond 26th Avenue [1][2]. On November 15 the Board of Supervisors approved the changes 12 to 5 [1]. The avenues were furious. Speakers mocked the 'unpronounceable' names and the Richmond Banner warned the districts would be called 'the Spanish Town of San Francisco' [2]. The Richmond had the city's oldest continuously operating improvement club, and it mobilised fast [1][2]. At a packed Saturday meeting on November 20, the commission backed down. The Examiner claimed thirty-five thousand residents had 'arose en masse' [2]. The avenues kept their numbers; only First Avenue (Arguello) and 49th Avenue (La Playa, 'the beach') changed [2]. The Richmond's lettered streets went through several drafts before settling on explorers after all: A, B and C streets became Anza, Balboa and Cabrillo [1][2].

title: The Champion's Camp at Seal Rock House

place.label: Site of Seal Rock House, foot of Sutro Heights, Point Lobos Ave and Great Highway

hook: In June 1910, the first Black heavyweight champion made his headquarters at an Ocean Beach roadhouse, training for the most racially charged fight in American history.
story: In 1910 former champion James J. Jeffries came out of retirement to fight Jack Johnson, the first African American heavyweight champion of the world. Jeffries said he was fighting 'for the sole purpose of proving that a white man is better than a Negro' [3]. Before the bout, Johnson set up his headquarters at Seal Rock House, a roadhouse at the foot of Sutro Heights, and trained at the Ocean Beach Pavilion nearby [1]. A photo dated June 26, 1910 shows him with his trainers outside the roadhouse [1]. It was taken by Percy Dana, a boxing photographer nicknamed 'Pee Wee' because he was so small, whose studio went on to be principal photographer for the fight [2]. On July 4, 1910, in Reno, Johnson won in the fifteenth round. Race riots broke out across the country, and more than 20 people died [3]. Films of the fight were banned in many places, and in 1912 Congress banned carrying fight films across state lines, a ban not lifted until 1940. Dana's photographs were for years one of the few ways to see the fight [2].

title: A Lifesavers' House Moves to Cabrillo Street
hook: The surfmen's motto was 'You have to go out. You don't have to come back.' One of their Victorian station buildings still stands as a Richmond house.
story: California's first lifesaving station opened in 1878 at Fulton Street and Great Highway, run by the U.S. Lifesaving Service. Its surfmen lived on site, ready to rescue crews from ships wrecked on Ocean Beach or the cliffs of Lands End. Their unofficial motto was grim: 'You have to go out. You don't have to come back' [1]. Crowds gathered to watch them drill. They fired lifelines from a small cannon to a fake ship's mast set in the sand, or rowed self-righting surfboats out past Seal Rocks, after horses hauled the boats across Great Highway on wheeled carts [1]. In 1914 the station became part of the new U.S. Coast Guard. In the 1920s the Coast Guard began replacing its aging Victorian buildings [1]. A former lifesaver, Carvel Torlakson, bought one of the 1870s buildings from the government for $75, moved it to a vacant lot at 47th Avenue and Cabrillo Street, set it on a new foundation and moved in [1]. The Western Neighborhoods Project dates the move to 1923 [2]. When John Martini wrote about it in 2015, it was still there [1].

title: From Nickel Rides to Playland

place.label: Chutes at the Beach / Playland site, Great Highway between Balboa and Fulton

hook: A carousel, a candy stand and a water chute grew into Playland at the Beach, taken over by two brothers who had learned showmanship in Melbourne.
story: In 1883 the Park and Ocean Railroad began bringing nickel-fare crowds to a terminus near today's La Playa and Balboa, where waffle stands, shooting galleries and carnival games soon gathered [1]. In the 1910s Charles Looff installed a carousel, and candy-stand operator John Friedle teamed up with Looff's son Arthur to build a real amusement park [1]. Sources differ on dates: the Western Neighborhoods Project says Chutes at the Beach opened in 1921 with the Big Dipper coaster following in 1922, while FoundSF puts the carousel building at 1912 and both rides at 1922 [1][2]. Admission was free [1]. Among the concessionaires was George K. Whitney, who with his brother Leo had run a shooting gallery in Melbourne, Australia, during World War I and developed a quick-finish photo process [3]. George opened a shooting gallery at the Chutes in the early 1920s and began buying up other leases [1][3]. In 1928 the Whitney brothers bought much of Friedle's investment and renamed the park Playland at the Beach [1]. 'Playland is a nickel and dime business,' George liked to say [3].

title: The New Balboa Lights Up the Avenues
hook: As the sand dunes filled with bungalows, a showman built an 800-seat neighbourhood movie palace on a street that barely escaped a different name.
story: By the mid-1920s the dunes of the Outer Richmond were filling with houses, and the new residents wanted movies close to home. Samuel H. Levin, whose San Francisco Theatres Inc. ran a chain of neighbourhood houses including the Alexandria and the Coliseum, opened the New Balboa Theatre near 38th Avenue with 800 seats [1][2]. Cinema Treasures gives the date as February 27, 1926, but Wikipedia cites an Examiner item dated June 27, 1926 announcing the opening 'tonight', so the exact day is uncertain [1][2]. It was designed by brothers James and Merritt Reid, whose credits included the Fairmont Hotel, the Spreckels Temple of Music in Golden Gate Park and the 1909 Cliff House about a mile away [1][3]. The theatre took its name from the explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa, like the street itself, which got that name in 1909 after the Richmond fought off a plan to rename its avenues [2][4]. The Levin family ran the Balboa for almost 60 years, until February 2001, and in 1966 and 1967 it showed The Sound of Music for 92 weeks [1]. It is still showing films today, one of the last neighbourhood theatres in the city [1].
